bull_bear.body:
- Leading market position as a community industrial gas provider - pioneer of India's community boiler system (first introduced in 2014) and, per F&S, the market leader in supply of steam through community boilers
- High barriers to entry - exclusive pipeline network already laid inside industrial clusters where limited space prevents a second distribution network being built
- Only company in India supplying nitrogen through a distributed pipeline network rather than cryogenic tanks or onsite generation (Source: F&S Report)
- Sticky, contracted customer base - customer supply arrangements of 12 months to 10 years, relationships in excess of three years with all top 10 steam customers, repeat customers at 88.01% of FY25 revenue and 96.64% in H1 FY26
- Customer base grown from 91 (FY23) to 174 (H1 FY26) with reputed clients such as Aether Industries, Anupam Rasayan India, Globe Enviro Care, Gujarat Polysol Chemicals, Orgo Chem Gujarat and Subhasri Pigments
- Eco-efficient asset base - AFBC boiler designs that cut fuel consumption and SOx/NOx emissions, waste-to-energy unit at Vapi burning plastic waste and textile chindi, hydrated lime dosing, turbine co-generation at Nandesari
- Technology-led monitoring - SCADA, flow meters, steam traps/auto valves and drone mapping of the 56,236 metre pipeline network for real-time leakage, pressure, temperature and emissions tracking
- Contractual pass-through of coal cost - pricing has a fixed component with annual escalation plus a variable component linked to coal price, so raw material price increases can be passed to customers
- Experienced promoter-led management with 29 years of textile and 10 years of community boiler experience, supported by executive directors and a CFO from banking and financial services
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Geographic and proximity lock-in — Every boiler and the nitrogen unit sit in Gujarat and gas can only be supplied to customers close enough to be pipeline-connected, so each facility's addressable market is a single industrial estate; growth depends on finding suitable land next to clusters and on securing and retaining pipeline rights-of-way from regulators, and there is limited physical space left for new pipelines in established estates.
- Customer concentration and contract churn — Top 10 customers were 53.95% of FY25 revenue and 52.83% in H1 FY26 with the largest alone at 23.65% in H1 FY26; contracts run 12 months to 10 years but there were instances of termination by the Company or the customer in FY25, and customers without written agreements buy on an invoice basis with no continuing obligation.
- Related party dependence on the Promoter's Sanjoo group — Transactions with Group Companies were 70.41% of FY25 revenue from operations and 61.72% in H1 FY26; Sanjoo Dyeing is simultaneously a top-10 customer, a top-10 supplier and the owner of the Sachin boilers the Company merely operates, so a large share of reported scale depends on entities controlled by the Promoter and on the continuation of arm's-length terms.
- Coal input dependence with import and supplier concentration — Coal was 76.19% of FY25 purchases and 77.97% in H1 FY26, sourced largely from Indian importers who buy Indonesian coal, with no long-term supply contracts and no FX hedging; top 10 suppliers were 91.52% of H1 FY26 purchases, so quantity or quality failure directly stops steam production even though price rises are contractually passed through.
- Leverage and capital intensity — Total borrowings were Rs 2,165.97 million as at September 30, 2025 (net debt/equity 1.42x) against net worth of Rs 1,396.70 million, with capex of Rs 1,055.36 million in FY25 alone and eight further projects planned; finance costs were 5.61% of FY25 revenue, and Rs 1,500.00 million of Fresh Issue proceeds are earmarked to repay debt, after which further expansion still requires debt or equity.
- Promoter share pledge tied to the Ascertis Credit debt — 148,874,167 Equity Shares (65.88% of paid-up capital) held by the Promoter were pledged as at the UDRHP-I date; the trustee has confirmed release before UDRHP-II filing but the shares must be repledged if the Ascertis Credit (formerly BPEA) debt is not repaid within an agreed timeline.
- Environmental and licensing exposure — The Company has previously operated a boiler before receiving final regulatory approval and received a GPCB show cause notice dated May 15, 2025 for haphazard plastic waste storage, exhaust leakages and a non-operational screw conveyor; boiler licences for the Vapi WTE unit expired on November 27, 2025 with renewal applications pending, and coal-fired operations remain exposed to tighter emission rules or fuel duties.
- Execution risk on the eight-project expansion — Capacity is planned to nearly double from 345 TPH to 675 TPH, yet Pirana and Tarapur did not have all approvals in place as at September 30, 2025, several projects have no customer tie-ups for the steam, funding is unappraised by any bank or independent agency, and utilisation is already only 45.58% (FY25), so delays, cost overruns or unfilled capacity would hit returns.

business.body: Steamhouse India generates steam in community boilers and distributes it, along with purchased third-party steam and separated/compressed nitrogen, through a dedicated pipeline network to industrial customers located in Gujarat's GIDC clusters. It operates seven community steam boilers (six owned, one leased) at Vapi Phase 1, Vapi WTE unit, Ankleshwar Phase 1 and 2, Sarigam, Nandesari and Panoli, plus one nitrogen facility at Ankleshwar, and distributes purchased steam at Dahej GIDC and Sachin GIDC. Customers are pharmaceutical, chemical, textile, agrochemical, tyre, dyes and pigments, polymer and paint manufacturers; the company also trades surplus coal bought in bulk for its own boilers.

- **Nitrogen:** Separation, compression and pipeline distribution of purified nitrogen; commenced February 1, 2025 (0.02% of FY25 revenue from operations)
- **Coal trading:** Trading of coal on an invoice-only basis from bulk coal procured as boiler fuel (19.30% of FY25 revenue from operations)

outlook.body:
- Expand capacity by setting up new community industrial gas facilities in and outside Gujarat - Nandesari (Phase 2), Jhagadia, Vapi (Phase 3), Dahej SEZ, Ankleshwar (Phase 3), Pirana (Ahmedabad), Panoli (Phase 2) and Tarapur - and participate in tenders for community gas systems in upcoming industrial parks across India
- Scale the asset-light 'purchase and distribution' model by partnering with industrial units that have unused or by-product steam, expanding distribution capacity with relatively lower capital expenditure
- Diversify business offerings - a hybrid own-plus-purchase steam model, modifying/operating/maintaining high-pressure boilers for industrial customers, expanding non-fossil fuel use, and generating and distributing other industrial gases such as hydrogen, instrument air and carbon dioxide

outlook.body: The Company plans eight new or expanded community industrial gas facilities - Nandesari (Phase 2, 30 TPH, non-fossil fuel), Jhagadia (30 TPH, coal), Vapi (Phase 3, 30 TPH, non-fossil fuel), Dahej SEZ (30 TPH, coal), Ankleshwar (Phase 3, 60 TPH, coal), Pirana/Ahmedabad (30 TPH, non-fossil fuel), Panoli (Phase 2, 60 TPH, coal) and Tarapur (60 TPH, coal). Once completed, steam distribution capacity rises from 345 TPH to 675 TPH, i.e. annual installed capacity from 2,185,920.00 TPA to 4,276,800.00 TPA (assuming 330 operational days and 80% boiler efficiency). Three of these projects are funded from the Fresh Issue: brownfield expansion of Ankleshwar (120 TPH to 180 TPH, cost Rs 350.99 million, targeted August 2027), brownfield expansion of Panoli (60 TPH to 120 TPH, cost Rs 357.99 million, targeted August 2027) and a greenfield 30 TPH plant at Dahej SEZ on 30-year licensed land (total cost Rs 427.07 million of which Rs 53.27 million already spent from internal accruals, targeted October 2027). Nandesari (Phase 2), Jhagadia and Vapi (Phase 3) are targeted to start operations in calendar year 2026 and Pirana and Tarapur in calendar year 2027, funded by debt/lease finance, internal accruals and, for Pirana, a Rs 347.50 million subsidy; Pirana and Tarapur did not have all relevant approvals in place as at September 30, 2025. Alongside owned capacity, the Company intends to keep adding purchase-and-distribution arrangements (Kilburn Chemicals at Dahej, Sanjoo Dyeing at Sachin) that expand distributed volume without building a boiler, and to widen the gas slate beyond steam and nitrogen to hydrogen, instrument air and carbon dioxide.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Coal is the primary fuel and the dominant cost - cost of goods sold was 78.94% of total expenses in FY25 and 80.54% in H1 FY26; coal purchases were 76.19% of total purchases in FY25 and 77.97% in H1 FY26
- Steam pricing is split into a fixed per-unit component with built-in annual escalation for inflation and a variable per-unit component linked to the coal price, so raw material price increases are contractually passed through to customers, though cash outflows can still rise
- Indirect FX exposure - coal is bought mostly from Indian importers who source from Indonesia, with no hedging; rupee weakness against the US dollar can raise input cost
- Customer concentration - top 10 customers were 53.95% of FY25 revenue and 52.83% in H1 FY26; largest customer 16.60% in FY25 and 23.65% in H1 FY26
- Supplier concentration - top 10 suppliers were 75.35% of purchases in FY25 and 91.52% in H1 FY26
- Capital intensity and cost of funding - capex of Rs 1,055.36 million in FY25 and Rs 493.67 million in H1 FY26; finance costs were 5.61% of revenue in FY25 (6.40% FY24, 2.96% FY23) and 4.63% in H1 FY26; borrowings priced at fixed rates of 8.14%-16.08% (banks/NCDs) and 6.72%-14.25% (NBFCs)
- Revenue mix shift - purchase and distribution of steam rose to 19.71% of FY25 revenue (0.00% in FY24) and coal trading to 19.30% (0.01% in FY24), while own generation and distribution of steam fell from 99.19% of FY24 revenue to 60.56% in FY25; reported EBITDA margin moved 23.45% (FY24) to 17.54% (FY25) to 14.08% (H1 FY26)
- Related party dependence - transactions with Group Companies equalled 70.41% of FY25 revenue from operations and 61.72% in H1 FY26 (98.88%-99.46% of all related party transactions)
- Geographic concentration - all generation assets and raw material suppliers are in Gujarat, and most planned expansion is also in Gujarat
- Capacity utilisation of industrial gases sold was 45.58% in FY25 (42.88% FY24, 57.00% FY23) and 42.63% in H1 FY26, so incremental volume can be served before new capacity is required
- Competition from renewable and alternative steam sources (biomass, nuclear, green hydrogen) and from potential new entrants in industrial gases

risks.note: Every boiler and the nitrogen unit sit in Gujarat and gas can only be supplied to customers close enough to be pipeline-connected, so each facility's addressable market is a single industrial estate; growth depends on finding suitable land next to clusters and on securing and retaining pipeline rights-of-way from regulators, and there is limited physical space left for new pipelines in established estates.

Top 10 customers were 53.95% of FY25 revenue and 52.83% in H1 FY26 with the largest alone at 23.65% in H1 FY26; contracts run 12 months to 10 years but there were instances of termination by the Company or the customer in FY25, and customers without written agreements buy on an invoice basis with no continuing obligation.

Transactions with Group Companies were 70.41% of FY25 revenue from operations and 61.72% in H1 FY26; Sanjoo Dyeing is simultaneously a top-10 customer, a top-10 supplier and the owner of the Sachin boilers the Company merely operates, so a large share of reported scale depends on entities controlled by the Promoter and on the continuation of arm's-length terms.
risks.risk: Related party dependence on the Promoter's Sanjoo group

risks.note: Coal was 76.19% of FY25 purchases and 77.97% in H1 FY26, sourced largely from Indian importers who buy Indonesian coal, with no long-term supply contracts and no FX hedging; top 10 suppliers were 91.52% of H1 FY26 purchases, so quantity or quality failure directly stops steam production even though price rises are contractually passed through.
risks.risk: Coal input dependence with import and supplier concentration

148,874,167 Equity Shares (65.88% of paid-up capital) held by the Promoter were pledged as at the UDRHP-I date; the trustee has confirmed release before UDRHP-II filing but the shares must be repledged if the Ascertis Credit (formerly BPEA) debt is not repaid within an agreed timeline.

Capacity is planned to nearly double from 345 TPH to 675 TPH, yet Pirana and Tarapur did not have all approvals in place as at September 30, 2025, several projects have no customer tie-ups for the steam, funding is unappraised by any bank or independent agency, and utilisation is already only 45.58% (FY25), so delays, cost overruns or unfilled capacity would hit returns.

orders_not_placed.note: The DRHP states verbatim, separately for each of the three capex objects: 'We are yet to place any order for plant and machinery. Further, the quotations received from vendors in relation to the proposed expansion are valid as on the date of this Updated Draft Red Herring Prospectus-I. We have not entered into any definitive agreements with any of the vendors...'. Every one of the component tables (boiler and boiler parts, plant and machinery, steel structure, electrical, instrument, labour, pipeline) carries the matching disclaimer that quotations have been received from several third-party vendors but no definitive agreements have been entered into with any of them. Accordingly every machinery line recorded above is a quotation only, not a placed order, and order_placed is false throughout. No percentage of capex is stated in the document and the DRHP's own capex totals for the three projects are the only stated aggregates, so pct_of_capex is left null rather than derived. A dedicated risk factor is cross-referenced on page 72: 'The Objects of the Offer include orders for equipment and machinery which have not yet been placed. Further, we are yet to place orders for capital expenditures. In the event of any delay in placement of such orders, the proposed schedule of implementation and deployment of the Net Proceeds may be extended or may vary'. Countervailing wording: the estimated costs are described as being based on 'quotations from suppliers or purchase orders issued to suppliers/vendors', but the document identifies no specific purchase order as issued. The DRHP also states no second-hand or used machinery is proposed to be purchased out of the Net Proceeds, and that the Promoters, Directors and Key Managerial Personnel have no interest in the proposed acquisition of the plant and machinery or in the entities providing the quotations. Quotation validity is a live constraint: most quotations are dated October 1-10, 2025 and valid for 8 months or 240 days, with the Thermax boiler quotations dated October 27, 2025 valid to April 30, 2026

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Steamhouse India generates steam in community boilers and distributes it, along with purchased third-party steam and separated/compressed nitrogen, through a dedicated pipeline network to industrial customers located in Gujarat's GIDC clusters. It operates seven community steam boilers (six owned, one leased) at Vapi Phase 1, Vapi WTE unit, Ankleshwar Phase 1 and 2, Sarigam, Nandesari and Panoli, plus one nitrogen facility at Ankleshwar, and distributes purchased steam at Dahej GIDC and Sachin GIDC. Customers are pharmaceutical, chemical, textile, agrochemical, tyre, dyes and pigments, polymer and paint manufacturers; the company also trades surplus coal bought in bulk for its own boilers.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Coal is the primary fuel and the dominant cost - cost of goods sold was 78.94% of total expenses in FY25 and 80.54% in H1 FY26; coal purchases were 76.19% of total purchases in FY25 and 77.97% in H1 FY26
- Steam pricing is split into a fixed per-unit component with built-in annual escalation for inflation and a variable per-unit component linked to the coal price, so raw material price increases are contractually passed through to customers, though cash outflows can still rise
- Indirect FX exposure - coal is bought mostly from Indian importers who source from Indonesia, with no hedging; rupee weakness against the US dollar can raise input cost
- Customer concentration - top 10 customers were 53.95% of FY25 revenue and 52.83% in H1 FY26; largest customer 16.60% in FY25 and 23.65% in H1 FY26
- Supplier concentration - top 10 suppliers were 75.35% of purchases in FY25 and 91.52% in H1 FY26
- Capital intensity and cost of funding - capex of Rs 1,055.36 million in FY25 and Rs 493.67 million in H1 FY26; finance costs were 5.61% of revenue in FY25 (6.40% FY24, 2.96% FY23) and 4.63% in H1 FY26; borrowings priced at fixed rates of 8.14%-16.08% (banks/NCDs) and 6.72%-14.25% (NBFCs)
- Revenue mix shift - purchase and distribution of steam rose to 19.71% of FY25 revenue (0.00% in FY24) and coal trading to 19.30% (0.01% in FY24), while own generation and distribution of steam fell from 99.19% of FY24 revenue to 60.56% in FY25; reported EBITDA margin moved 23.45% (FY24) to 17.54% (FY25) to 14.08% (H1 FY26)
- Related party dependence - transactions with Group Companies equalled 70.41% of FY25 revenue from operations and 61.72% in H1 FY26 (98.88%-99.46% of all related party transactions)
- Geographic concentration - all generation assets and raw material suppliers are in Gujarat, and most planned expansion is also in Gujarat
- Capacity utilisation of industrial gases sold was 45.58% in FY25 (42.88% FY24, 57.00% FY23) and 42.63% in H1 FY26, so incremental volume can be served before new capacity is required
- Competition from renewable and alternative steam sources (biomass, nuclear, green hydrogen) and from potential new entrants in industrial gases

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Expand capacity by setting up new community industrial gas facilities in and outside Gujarat - Nandesari (Phase 2), Jhagadia, Vapi (Phase 3), Dahej SEZ, Ankleshwar (Phase 3), Pirana (Ahmedabad), Panoli (Phase 2) and Tarapur - and participate in tenders for community gas systems in upcoming industrial parks across India
- Scale the asset-light 'purchase and distribution' model by partnering with industrial units that have unused or by-product steam, expanding distribution capacity with relatively lower capital expenditure
- Diversify business offerings - a hybrid own-plus-purchase steam model, modifying/operating/maintaining high-pressure boilers for industrial customers, expanding non-fossil fuel use, and generating and distributing other industrial gases such as hydrogen, instrument air and carbon dioxide
- Continue to focus on operational efficiency and reduce operating expenses through bulk coal purchases, reuse of bed material, variable frequency drives on fans and pumps, turbine installation and drone-based mapping
- Improve the debt profile by using Rs 1,500.00 million of Net Proceeds to repay or prepay borrowings, lowering debt servicing costs and freeing internal accruals for growth
- Reduce carbon footprint by shifting to non-fossil fuels (industrial/plastic waste, textile chindi, RDF, agro-waste, waste gas), exploring a ground-mounted solar plant across existing and upcoming facilities, and potentially becoming eligible for carbon credits under India's carbon credit trading scheme

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: The Company plans eight new or expanded community industrial gas facilities - Nandesari (Phase 2, 30 TPH, non-fossil fuel), Jhagadia (30 TPH, coal), Vapi (Phase 3, 30 TPH, non-fossil fuel), Dahej SEZ (30 TPH, coal), Ankleshwar (Phase 3, 60 TPH, coal), Pirana/Ahmedabad (30 TPH, non-fossil fuel), Panoli (Phase 2, 60 TPH, coal) and Tarapur (60 TPH, coal). Once completed, steam distribution capacity rises from 345 TPH to 675 TPH, i.e. annual installed capacity from 2,185,920.00 TPA to 4,276,800.00 TPA (assuming 330 operational days and 80% boiler efficiency). Three of these projects are funded from the Fresh Issue: brownfield expansion of Ankleshwar (120 TPH to 180 TPH, cost Rs 350.99 million, targeted August 2027), brownfield expansion of Panoli (60 TPH to 120 TPH, cost Rs 357.99 million, targeted August 2027) and a greenfield 30 TPH plant at Dahej SEZ on 30-year licensed land (total cost Rs 427.07 million of which Rs 53.27 million already spent from internal accruals, targeted October 2027). Nandesari (Phase 2), Jhagadia and Vapi (Phase 3) are targeted to start operations in calendar year 2026 and Pirana and Tarapur in calendar year 2027, funded by debt/lease finance, internal accruals and, for Pirana, a Rs 347.50 million subsidy; Pirana and Tarapur did not have all relevant approvals in place as at September 30, 2025. Alongside owned capacity, the Company intends to keep adding purchase-and-distribution arrangements (Kilburn Chemicals at Dahej, Sanjoo Dyeing at Sachin) that expand distributed volume without building a boiler, and to widen the gas slate beyond steam and nitrogen to hydrogen, instrument air and carbon dioxide.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Leading market position as a community industrial gas provider - pioneer of India's community boiler system (first introduced in 2014) and, per F&S, the market leader in supply of steam through community boilers
- High barriers to entry - exclusive pipeline network already laid inside industrial clusters where limited space prevents a second distribution network being built
- Only company in India supplying nitrogen through a distributed pipeline network rather than cryogenic tanks or onsite generation (Source: F&S Report)
- Sticky, contracted customer base - customer supply arrangements of 12 months to 10 years, relationships in excess of three years with all top 10 steam customers, repeat customers at 88.01% of FY25 revenue and 96.64% in H1 FY26
- Customer base grown from 91 (FY23) to 174 (H1 FY26) with reputed clients such as Aether Industries, Anupam Rasayan India, Globe Enviro Care, Gujarat Polysol Chemicals, Orgo Chem Gujarat and Subhasri Pigments
- Eco-efficient asset base - AFBC boiler designs that cut fuel consumption and SOx/NOx emissions, waste-to-energy unit at Vapi burning plastic waste and textile chindi, hydrated lime dosing, turbine co-generation at Nandesari
- Technology-led monitoring - SCADA, flow meters, steam traps/auto valves and drone mapping of the 56,236 metre pipeline network for real-time leakage, pressure, temperature and emissions tracking
- Contractual pass-through of coal cost - pricing has a fixed component with annual escalation plus a variable component linked to coal price, so raw material price increases can be passed to customers
- Experienced promoter-led management with 29 years of textile and 10 years of community boiler experience, supported by executive directors and a CFO from banking and financial services

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Geographic and proximity lock-in — Every boiler and the nitrogen unit sit in Gujarat and gas can only be supplied to customers close enough to be pipeline-connected, so each facility's addressable market is a single industrial estate; growth depends on finding suitable land next to clusters and on securing and retaining pipeline rights-of-way from regulators, and there is limited physical space left for new pipelines in established estates.
- Customer concentration and contract churn — Top 10 customers were 53.95% of FY25 revenue and 52.83% in H1 FY26 with the largest alone at 23.65% in H1 FY26; contracts run 12 months to 10 years but there were instances of termination by the Company or the customer in FY25, and customers without written agreements buy on an invoice basis with no continuing obligation.
- Related party dependence on the Promoter's Sanjoo group — Transactions with Group Companies were 70.41% of FY25 revenue from operations and 61.72% in H1 FY26; Sanjoo Dyeing is simultaneously a top-10 customer, a top-10 supplier and the owner of the Sachin boilers the Company merely operates, so a large share of reported scale depends on entities controlled by the Promoter and on the continuation of arm's-length terms.
- Coal input dependence with import and supplier concentration — Coal was 76.19% of FY25 purchases and 77.97% in H1 FY26, sourced largely from Indian importers who buy Indonesian coal, with no long-term supply contracts and no FX hedging; top 10 suppliers were 91.52% of H1 FY26 purchases, so quantity or quality failure directly stops steam production even though price rises are contractually passed through.
- Leverage and capital intensity — Total borrowings were Rs 2,165.97 million as at September 30, 2025 (net debt/equity 1.42x) against net worth of Rs 1,396.70 million, with capex of Rs 1,055.36 million in FY25 alone and eight further projects planned; finance costs were 5.61% of FY25 revenue, and Rs 1,500.00 million of Fresh Issue proceeds are earmarked to repay debt, after which further expansion still requires debt or equity.
- Promoter share pledge tied to the Ascertis Credit debt — 148,874,167 Equity Shares (65.88% of paid-up capital) held by the Promoter were pledged as at the UDRHP-I date; the trustee has confirmed release before UDRHP-II filing but the shares must be repledged if the Ascertis Credit (formerly BPEA) debt is not repaid within an agreed timeline.
- Environmental and licensing exposure — The Company has previously operated a boiler before receiving final regulatory approval and received a GPCB show cause notice dated May 15, 2025 for haphazard plastic waste storage, exhaust leakages and a non-operational screw conveyor; boiler licences for the Vapi WTE unit expired on November 27, 2025 with renewal applications pending, and coal-fired operations remain exposed to tighter emission rules or fuel duties.
- Execution risk on the eight-project expansion — Capacity is planned to nearly double from 345 TPH to 675 TPH, yet Pirana and Tarapur did not have all approvals in place as at September 30, 2025, several projects have no customer tie-ups for the steam, funding is unappraised by any bank or independent agency, and utilisation is already only 45.58% (FY25), so delays, cost overruns or unfilled capacity would hit returns.
